codes.explanation:
You tried to reach past the end of an array

Turf arrays have a fixed size you choose when you declare them, and their valid indices always start at 0 and stop at `size - 1` -- never at `size` itself. So an array of 3 things has valid indices 0, 1, and 2, not 3.

    immut primes: int[3] = [2, 3, 5];
    mut first: int = primes[0];   // correct -- the first element
    mut last: int = primes[2];    // correct -- the last element (size - 1)

A negative index counts back from the end, so `primes[-1]` is that same last element and `primes[-3]` is the first. The valid range is `-3` to `2` -- an index below `-3` is out of bounds just like one above `2`:

    mut also_last: int = primes[-1];   // correct -- the last element
    mut oops2: int = primes[-4];       // there is no primes[-4]!

If you ask for one index too many:

    mut oops: int = primes[3];   // there is no primes[3]!

Turf catches this at compile time and tells you exactly how big the array actually is, so you don't have to go count the brackets yourself.

This mistake almost always comes from an off-by-one: thinking of "3 elements" as meaning "indices 1 through 3" (like counting objects) instead of "indices 0 through 2" (like counting positions). It's one of the most common trips in programming in general, not just in Turf -- you'll stop making it once counting from 0 feels natural, which usually doesn't take long.

If you actually need more room in the array, the fix isn't to index further -- it's to make the array bigger and give it the extra value:

    immut primes: int[4] = [2, 3, 5, 7];
    mut last: int = primes[3];   // now valid -- the array really has 4 slots

codes.title: Array bounds

codes.title: Index must be an integer

codes.explanation:
The number of values you gave doesn't match the array's declared size

When you declare an array with a size, like `int[3]`, and give it a list of starting values, the number of values in that list has to match the size exactly -- not more, not fewer.

    immut primes: int[3] = [2, 3, 5];   // correct -- 3 values for size 3

If you give too many or too few:

    immut primes: int[3] = [2, 3, 5, 7];   // 4 values, but size is 3

Turf won't quietly drop the extra value or leave a slot empty -- it stops and tells you exactly how many values it expected versus how many you gave, so nothing about your array's contents is left ambiguous.

To fix it, just make the two numbers agree. Either change the size to match your list:

    immut primes: int[4] = [2, 3, 5, 7];

...or trim the list to match the size:

    immut primes: int[3] = [2, 3, 5];

Either way works -- pick whichever one actually reflects what you meant the array to hold. This is an easy one to fix once you spot the mismatch, and Turf tells you both numbers up front so you don't have to go count them yourself.
codes.name: ArraySizeMismatchError
codes.title: Array size mismatch

codes.explanation:
One of the values in your array's initializer list is the wrong type

An array holds one specific type of value -- an `int[3]` holds three ints, a `string[2]` holds two strings, and so on. If even one value in the initializer list doesn't match that type, Turf catches it right away instead of letting a mixed-up array sneak into your program.

    immut primes: int[3] = [2, 3, 5];   // correct -- every value is an int

If one of the values is the wrong type:

    immut primes: int[3] = [2, 3, "five"];   // "five" is a string, not an int

Turf tells you the element type the array holds and the type of the value it found, so you know what to look for when you scan the list for the odd one out.

Either side can be the mistake: the values, or the type written for the array. When every value has the same type, the hint names both fixes:

    mut codes: char[3] = [10, 20, 30];
    // Hint: Declare `codes` as `int[3]`, or convert each value with `to char`.

If the values are what you meant, change the declaration (`mut codes: int[3]`). If the type is, make the values that type: convert them with `to` where a conversion exists, or write values of that type where none does (`mut flags: bool[2] = [1, 2];` needs `bool` values, since an `int` does not convert to a `bool`).

This is a great one to double-check whenever you're typing out a long list of values by hand -- it's easy for one typo (like quoting a number by accident) to slip in.

codes.explanation:
E015 is retired -- Turf now gives a more specific code

Older versions of Turf used this one code for every "the shape of this code isn't right" mistake: a missing punctuation mark, a bracket that is never closed, a name or type that is missing. Nothing produces E015 any more. If you are reading an old log, or an old tutorial, that is why you found it.

Each of those mistakes now has its own code, and its own explanation, so you are told *which* shape is wrong:

    E099  a string or character literal was never closed
    E100  an escape sequence Turf doesn't know (like `\q`)
    E101  a character literal that isn't exactly one character
    E102  a missing semicolon `;`
    E103  something that doesn't belong at this spot
    E104  a bracket, brace or parenthesis that is never closed
    E105  a missing comma
    E106  a missing colon
    E107  a missing opening `{` or `(`
    E108  a name was expected (a variable, function, field, ...)
    E109  a type was expected
    E110  a specific word or symbol was expected (`in`, `while`, `->`, ...)
    E111  code nested too deeply
    E112  `void` used as the type of a variable, field or parameter
    E113  syntax that used to exist and has been replaced
    E114  the same name declared twice inside a struct, enum, error or machine
    E115  an operator declared with the wrong number of operands
    E116  an `extern` function written with a body
    E117  an `error` declaration that mixes the `;` and `{ }` forms
    E118  a statement outside any function
    E119  no `main` function
    E120  a `for` loop form that isn't supported
    E123  an array size that isn't a positive whole number

Run `turf --explain` with the code your error shows.

codes.explanation:
`export mut` isn't a thing yet -- only `export immut` is

Turf lets you share a constant value across multiple files with `export immut`, but it doesn't yet support sharing a value that other files could change -- a true mutable global. So writing `export mut` trips this error, even though a plain, non-exported `mut` variable is completely normal everywhere else in Turf.

    export mut counter: int = 0;

This looks reasonable, but `counter` being both `mut` (changeable) and shared across files at the same time isn't supported. If you just need a constant that many files can read, swap `mut` for `immut`:

    export immut MAX_USERS: int = 100;

Now every file that imports this one can read `MAX_USERS`, and since it's `immut`, there's no ambiguity about who's allowed to change it (nobody -- that's the point).

If you genuinely need a value that changes and is visible everywhere, that's not something `export` can do for you right now. The usual workaround is to keep the mutable value local to one file and let other files interact with it through a function you write yourself -- something like a `get_counter()`/`set_counter()` pair -- rather than reaching in and changing it directly. It's a bit more typing, but it also means you always know exactly which piece of code is allowed to change the value, which tends to save you from confusing bugs down the road anyway.

codes.explanation:
That module function exists, but not for the arguments you gave it

Turf found the function you're calling -- the name is right -- but none of its declared versions accept the arguments you passed. Some functions in Turf have more than one version (called overloads) so they can work with different types, and this error means none of those versions match what you gave it.

    math::abs(true);

`math::abs` exists, but it only knows how to take an `int` or a `double` -- there's no version that accepts a `bool`. Turf tells you it found `abs`, just not one that fits a boolean argument.

    math::abs(-5);      // works -- matches the int version
    math::abs(-5.0);     // works -- matches the double version

If this happens to you, the fix is almost always to double check what type you're actually passing, and either pass a value of a type the function really supports, or convert your value first:

    mut flag: bool = true;
    mut as_number: int = 1;   // convert however makes sense for your case
    math::abs(as_number);

One small syntax reminder while you're here: module functions are always called with `::`, like `math::abs(...)`, never with a dot like `math.abs(...)` -- a dot is only for accessing fields and methods on a struct instance you're holding, not for module functions.
codes.name: ModuleArityOrTypeError
codes.title: No matching overload

codes.explanation:
That module doesn't have a function with this name

Turf found the module you're calling into just fine -- it just couldn't find a function by that name inside it. This is almost always a typo, and Turf is usually able to guess what you meant and suggest it.

    io::pritn("hello");

`io` is a real module, but it has no function called `pritn` -- it's missing a letter. Turf will tell you it thinks you meant `printline`, and once you fix the spelling it compiles right away:

    io::printline("hello");

If Turf's suggestion doesn't look right, or it doesn't have one, double-check two things: that you spelled the function name exactly as it's declared (function names are case-sensitive), and that the function actually lives in the module you're calling it on -- it's easy to remember a function existing "somewhere in the standard library" without remembering which specific module it's in.

This is different from the module itself not existing (that's a separate error) -- here, Turf already found and understood `io` just fine. It's only the function name after the `::` that it couldn't match.
codes.name: ModuleMethodNotFoundError
codes.title: Module method not found

codes.explanation:
Turf couldn't find a module by this name anywhere

When you write `import module_name;`, Turf looks for a file called `module_name.tr`, both in the standard library and in your own project. This error means it searched and simply couldn't find one anywhere.

    import strnigs;

There's no module called `strnigs` -- it's a typo for `strings`, one of Turf's standard library modules. Fixing the spelling solves it:

    import strings;

The most common causes of this error, in order of how often they actually happen:

  - A typo in the module name -- by far the most common cause, exactly like the example above.
  - You meant to write your own module, but the file doesn't exist yet, or it's named differently than you think (module names match the `.tr` filename exactly, without the `.tr` extension).
  - You meant a standard library module but got the name slightly wrong -- it's worth double-checking the exact name if you're not sure (for example, it's `strings`, not `string`).

If none of those explain it and you're confident the file really does exist, it's worth checking that your project's search setup is pointing at the right place -- but for the vast majority of the time you'll see this error, it really is just a small typo in the module name.

codes.explanation:
You tried to transition a state machine to a state it can't reach from here

Turf's `machine` construct lets you declare a set of states and the only legal moves between them. Once you write `machine ConnectionState { Idle -> Connecting, Connecting -> Connected, ... }`, that arrow list is the whole rulebook -- Turf checks every `.transition(...)` call against it.

This particular error happens inside a `compare`/`matches` block, where Turf already knows exactly which state you're in:

    machine ConnectionState {
        Idle -> Connecting,
        Connecting -> Connected,
        Connecting -> Failed,
        Connected -> Closing,
        Closing -> Idle,
    }

    mut conn: ConnectionState = ConnectionState::Idle;
    compare conn {
        matches ConnectionState::Idle:
            conn.transition(ConnectionState::Connecting);   // fine -- Idle -> Connecting exists
        done
        otherwise:
            mut noop: int = 0;
    }

If you try to jump somewhere that isn't listed:

    matches ConnectionState::Idle:
        conn.transition(ConnectionState::Closing);   // there's no Idle -> Closing edge!
    done

...Turf catches it right away, at compile time, instead of letting your program crash later when it actually tries to make that jump.

Two ways to fix it:

  - If the jump really should be allowed, add it to the machine's declaration: `Idle -> Closing,`.
  - If it shouldn't be allowed, that's Turf doing its job -- pick a state your current one can actually reach.

State machines are one of the pickier parts of Turf to get right at first, but this exact error is the compiler catching a real bug for you before it ever runs -- that's a win, not a setback.

E037 is retired -- an unknown function is E041

This code was defined for "I can't find a function named this", but nothing in the compiler ever produced it: a call to a function Turf doesn't know has always been reported as E041 ("Unknown function"). The number is kept so an old log that mentions it still has somewhere to land, and is never reused.

    mut n: int = lenght("hello");     // misspelled -- E041, with a "did you mean" suggestion

Run `turf --explain E041` for the explanation. In short: check the spelling, and check that you have imported the module the function lives in.

codes.title: No such variant

codes.explanation:
I can't find anything with that name

Turf looked everywhere it knows to look -- the current block, any block around it, the whole file -- and couldn't find anything called by that name. No variable, no struct, no enum, nothing. This is the most common error you'll hit while learning, and it's almost always one of two very fixable things.

The first is a plain typo:

    mut count: int = 0;
    count = coutn + 1;   // typo! should be "count"

If there's something similar already declared nearby, Turf will usually notice and suggest it for you right in the error message, so you can just apply the fix it's pointing at.

The second is forgetting to declare the variable at all before using it:

    mut n: int = undeclared_variable;   // this was never created anywhere

In Turf, you always create a variable with `mut` or `immut` before you can use it -- there's no way to just start using a name and have it exist automatically:

    mut undeclared_variable: int = 5;
    mut n: int = undeclared_variable;   // now this works

There is a third case, and the error's hint says so when it applies: the name IS declared, but as a type. A struct, enum or error type is not a value, so it can't stand alone in an expression:

    struct Node { v: int }
    mut a: int = Node;        // 'Node' is a struct, not a value

To get a value of a struct type, build one with `Node::default()` (or `Node::new(...)` if the struct declares a `.new` method); for an enum, name one of its variants, `Color::Red`.

If none of those is it, one more thing worth checking: is the name something from a module you haven't imported yet? A function or type that lives in another module needs `import` (or the right `::` qualifier) before Turf can see it. Once the name resolves to something real, this error clears right up.
codes.name: ReferenceError
codes.title: Unknown name

codes.explanation:
I don't know a function by that name

You called a function -- something with parentheses after it, like `do_something()` -- and Turf couldn't find any function with that exact name anywhere it looked: not in this file, not among the built-ins, not through anything you've imported.

    fn greet(name: string): void {
        printline("Hello, " + name);
    }

    greet("world");   // works -- "greet" is declared right above

Usually this is just a small typo in the function's name:

    grete("world");   // typo! should be "greet"

Just like with variable names, Turf will often notice a close match nearby and suggest it for you, so check the error message for a suggestion before anything else.

If it's not a typo, the function might genuinely not exist yet in your code (you can write it yourself with `fn`), or it might live in a standard-library module you haven't imported. Things like `strings::length(...)` or `mem::malloc(...)` need their module imported first with `import strings;` or `import mem;` before Turf can see them. Once the name matches something real and reachable, you're good to go.

One more cause, specific to types: Turf has no constructor-call syntax, so `Node(5)` for a struct named `Node` is an unknown function too -- the error's hint says so when that is what happened. Build the value with `Node::new(5)` (if `Node` declares a `.new` method) or `Node::default()`, and for an enum or error type name one of its variants (`Color::Red`).

codes.title: Unknown function

codes.name: UnknownTypeError
codes.title: Unknown type

codes.explanation:
You're using this variable before you've actually created it

Turf runs your code from top to bottom, one statement at a time -- so a variable has to be declared with `mut` or `immut` BEFORE you can use it, not after. This error means Turf found a real, valid declaration for the name you used... it's just further down in the same block, after the line that tried to use it.

    mut y: int = x + 1;   // x doesn't exist yet at this point!
    mut x: int = 5;       // x is only created here, one line too late

The fix is simply to reorder things so the declaration comes first:

    mut x: int = 5;
    mut y: int = x + 1;   // now x already exists by the time we use it

This is an easy one to trip on when you're moving code around or writing things in a different order than you first thought of them -- nothing to worry about, just swap the two lines (or move the declaration up) and you're done. If it turns out the name is a typo instead of a real ordering issue, Turf's other unknown-name error will usually catch that case and suggest the right name instead.
codes.name: UseBeforeDeclarationError
codes.title: Use before declaration

codes.explanation:
You called a function with the wrong number of arguments

Turf found the function you're calling just fine -- the name is right -- but none of its versions take the number of arguments you gave it. This is one of the friendlier errors to fix, because the compiler prints out every valid way to call that function right in the error message.

For example, if `add` is declared like this:

    fn add(a: int, b: int): int {
        return a + b;
    }

...then calling it with three arguments instead of two will trigger this error:

    add(2, 3, 4);   // ERROR: I found no overload of `add` that takes 3 arguments.

The fix is almost always just counting again -- look at the "Known overloads" list the error prints, and match your call to one of them exactly. Either you added or forgot an argument, or the function's own declaration needs to change if it's supposed to accept a different number of values.

Sometimes the compiler can work out the edit for you and prints it as a `Fix:`. With one argument too many, it tries removing each argument in turn; if exactly one removal leaves arguments that fit, that is the fix. Above, `add(2, 3, 4)` gets none, because removing any of the three leaves two ints. With one argument too few, it passes a variable that has the missing parameter's name, if one is in scope: `area(width)` becomes `area(width, height)` when a `height` variable exists.

One thing worth knowing about: if you're calling a method on a struct instance with `.` (like `thing.method(x)`) and that method is declared `static`, the argument count can look off by one in a confusing way, because `.` normally passes the instance itself in as a hidden first argument that a `static` method doesn't expect. If that's what's happening, Turf will usually catch it and tell you directly rather than leaving you to puzzle over a mismatched count -- but it's worth keeping in mind if the numbers don't seem to add up.
codes.name: WrongArityError
codes.title: Wrong number of arguments

codes.explanation:
You tried to construct a struct through an existing instance instead of its type

In Turf, `new` and `default` are special -- they're the only two ways to build a struct, and they're always called on the struct's TYPE NAME with `::`, never on a variable you already have with `.`. Even though `.new` looks like it's declared as a normal method internally, calling it is reserved specifically for construction.

Here's the correct way to build a struct:

    mut p: Point = Point::new(1, 2);
    mut d: Point = Point::default();

If you already have a `Point` called `p` and try to call `.new(...)` or `.default()` on it directly, Turf stops you:

    p.new(3, 4);      // ERROR: I cannot call `new` on an instance with `.`.
    p.default();       // ERROR: I cannot call `default` on an instance with `.`.

It's an easy slip to make, especially if you're used to languages where "calling a constructor again" on an existing object is a normal thing to do. In Turf it isn't -- construction always makes a brand-new value, and it always goes through `::` on the type name, not `.` on a variable.

If what you actually wanted was to reset an existing instance's fields back to some starting values, that's not something `new`/`default` do for you automatically -- write your own ordinary method (with any name other than `new` or `default`) that assigns the fields you want, and call that through `.` like any other method.
codes.name: ConstructorCalledOnInstanceError
codes.title: Constructor called on instance

codes.name: ConstructorCannotBeStaticError
codes.title: Constructor cannot be static

codes.explanation:
You passed arguments to default(), but it never takes any

`StructName::default()` is a special constructor that Turf generates for you automatically -- it just sets every field on the struct back to its zero value (0 for numbers, empty for strings, and so on). Because it doesn't do anything with input values, it never accepts any arguments at all, not even zero of some and some of others -- always exactly none.

This is the correct way to call it:

    mut p: Point = Point::default();

Passing anything in triggers this error:

    mut p: Point = Point::default(1, 2);   // ERROR: `Point::default()` takes no arguments, but I got 2.

If you want a struct built with specific starting values instead of all zeros, `default()` isn't the tool for that -- you want `StructName::new(...)` instead, which is where you (or whoever wrote the struct) define exactly what arguments it takes:

    mut p: Point = Point::new(1, 2);

Just swapping `default` for `new` (assuming the struct has a `.new` defined) is usually all it takes to fix this.
codes.name: DefaultConstructorArityError
codes.title: Arguments passed to default()

codes.explanation:
You used '.' on something that isn't an actual instance

Turf has one consistent rule: `.` is only for reaching into a real instance you're holding -- a variable that actually contains a value. Anything else -- a module name, or a struct's bare type name used without an instance -- needs `::` instead. This error means you used `.` on one of those "anything else" cases.

The two most common ways to hit this:

    io.printline("hi");   // ERROR -- 'io' is a module, not an instance
    Point.origin();        // ERROR -- 'Point' is a struct type, not an instance

Both are fixed the same way -- just swap `.` for `::`:

    io::printline("hi");
    Point::origin();

A quick way to tell which one you need: if you can point at an actual value on the left (something you got back from `Point::new(...)` or `Point::default()`, stored in a variable), that value's fields and methods use `.`. Everything else -- the module itself, or the type name on its own -- always uses `::`. So `p.sum()` is right if `p` is a real `Point` you're holding, but `Point.origin()` is never right, because `Point` there is just the type's name, not a value.

codes.explanation:
E055 is retired -- a bad argument to abs() is now reported as E056 or E025

Older versions of Turf treated `abs` as a compiler built-in with an error of its own. It is an ordinary function in the standard library now (`math::abs`), like every other, so nothing produces E055 any more. The number is kept so that an old log or tutorial that mentions it still has somewhere to land, and is never reused for anything else.

Passing `abs` something that isn't a number is reported like any other call with the wrong argument types:

    mut bad: int = math::abs("negative five");

That gives `E025`: Turf found `math::abs`, and none of its versions take a `string`. `abs` has one version for `int` and one for `double`:

    mut n: int = math::abs(-5);          // 5
    mut d: double = math::abs(-3.14);    // 3.14

Run `turf --explain E025` for the full explanation.

codes.title: Wrong argument type

codes.explanation:
You used an operator on a kind of value it doesn't work for

Operators have a job: `+ - * / %` do arithmetic on numbers, `& | ^ << >>` work on whole numbers, `&&` and `||` combine two `bool`s, `!` flips a `bool`, `~` flips the bits of an int. If a value isn't the kind the operator works on -- a `string`, a struct, a `bool` where a number belongs -- Turf can't tell what the operation is supposed to mean, so it stops and names the operator and the two types.

This works:

    mut sum: int = 3 + 4;
    mut avg: double = 7.0 / 2.0;

This doesn't, because `"4"` is text, not a number:

    mut bad: int = 3 + "4";            // cannot apply '+' to 'int' and 'string'

The same goes for the shorthand forms (`x += "4"`), `x++` on a string, `n && m` or `!n` on ints (write `n != 0`), and `**` or `&` on a type that isn't a number.

To fix it, make both sides genuinely the kind the operator wants. If you have a number stored as text you need an actual numeric value first -- Turf doesn't parse text into numbers on its own.

If you wanted to *join* two pieces of text, `+` on two strings does that; it is a number and a string that can't be mixed.

A struct can get its own `+` (or `==`, `[]`, ...) by declaring an `operator`; without one, the operators above don't apply to it.

(Division or remainder by a literal zero is a different thing: Turf warns about it at compile time -- "this will crash at runtime" -- and the program stops when it runs. It is not this error.)
codes.name: ArithmeticError
codes.title: Operator applied to the wrong kind of value

codes.explanation:
You assigned null to a variable that isn't a pointer

`null` means "no value yet," and in Turf that concept only applies to pointer types -- variables declared with a `*` in their type, like `int*`. A plain `int`, `double`, `bool`, `string`, `char`, or ordinary struct always holds a real value; there's no such thing as an "empty" one of those, so `null` doesn't make sense for them.

This is fine, because `ptr` is a pointer type:

    mut ptr: int* = null;

This isn't, because `n` is a plain `int`, not a pointer:

    mut n: int = null;

Turf tells you the variable's actual declared type, so you can see right away why `null` doesn't fit there.

If you really wanted a placeholder value you can check for later, you'll need to declare the variable as a pointer type (`int*` instead of `int`). If you just wanted a normal starting value, skip the `= null` entirely -- declaring a variable without an initializer already gives it a sensible default (zero for numbers, false for bools, and so on), which is almost always what you actually want here.

codes.explanation:
E063 is retired -- a bad argument to power() is now reported as E056 or E025

Older versions of Turf treated `power` as a compiler built-in with an error of its own. It is an ordinary function in the standard library now (`math::power`), like every other, so nothing produces E063 any more. The number is kept so that an old log or tutorial that mentions it still has somewhere to land, and is never reused for anything else.

Passing `power` something that isn't a number is reported like any other call with the wrong argument types:

    mut bad: int = math::power(true, 2);

That gives `E025`: Turf found `math::power`, and none of its versions take a `bool`. `power` is defined for numbers -- an `int` or a `double` for each of the base and the exponent:

    mut a: int = math::power(2, 10);          // 1024
    mut b: double = math::power(2.0, 0.5);    // the square root of 2

Run `turf --explain E025` for the full explanation.

codes.explanation:
You tried to convert something to a string that Turf doesn't know how to convert

Turf's `expr to string` conversion only understands a small, specific set of types: whole numbers, decimal numbers, and true/false values.

    mut s1: string = 42 to string;      // "42"
    mut s2: string = 3.14 to string;    // "3.14"
    mut s3: string = true to string;    // "true"

If you try it on something else, like a whole struct:

    mut bad: string = my_struct to string;

...Turf tells you which type it couldn't convert, because there's no automatic, one-size-fits-all way to turn an arbitrary struct into readable text -- it doesn't know which fields you'd want shown, or in what order.

The fix is to build the string yourself out of the pieces that ARE convertible. You can combine strings with `+`, so something like this works today:

    mut description: string = "x=" + (p.x to string) + ", y=" + (p.y to string);

If you find yourself doing this for the same struct in a lot of places, it's worth writing a small helper function that takes the struct and returns the formatted `string`, so you only have to write the field-by-field logic once.

codes.explanation:
You tried to use a field that doesn't exist on this struct

Every struct in Turf only has the fields you declared for it -- nothing more. If you write `something.some_field` and `some_field` was never listed in that struct's `{ }` block, the compiler stops you right here, before your program can run with a value that was never really there.

The most common reason this happens is a simple typo. Here's a struct with a `password` field:

    struct User {
        password: string
    }

    mut u: User = User::new("secret");
    mut pw: string = u.password;   // correct -- reads the real field

If you accidentally typed the field name wrong:

    mut pw: string = u.pasword;   // typo!

...Turf will tell you exactly which field it thinks you meant, so you can just fix the spelling and move on.

A couple of other things worth checking if it's NOT a typo:

  - Are you accessing the field on the right variable? It's easy to mix up two structs that have similarly-named fields.
  - Did you mean to call a method instead? `u.password` and `u.password()` are different things -- one reads a stored value, the other calls a function. If `password` is meant to be a method, make sure it's declared as one (with `fn User.password(): ...`), not as a field.
  - If the field really should exist and just hasn't been added yet, you can add it straight to the struct's declaration:

    struct User {
        password: string,
        email: string   // new field -- comma-separated, just like this
    }

Once the field name matches exactly what the struct declares, this error goes away and your code compiles like normal. This is a very normal thing to run into while you're still learning your way around a struct's shape -- nothing to worry about.

The same code covers a field on something that is not a struct at all: a `string`, an `int`, an enum, an array. Those have no fields, so no name is right:

    mut s: string = "abc";
    mut n: int = s.size;          // a string has no fields

If you meant a method, call it with parentheses (`s.length()`), or use the functions in `strings::`.

codes.explanation:
Your struct contains itself by value, and that has no finite size

Every struct's size has to be computable just from its own declaration --
the compiler needs to know exactly how many bytes to reserve for it before
it can ever create one. A struct that holds ITSELF as a plain field breaks
that completely: to know how big `A` is, the compiler would first need to
know how big `A` is, forever, with no base case. There's no such thing as a
struct that's "infinitely big", so this is rejected before your program can
ever try to create one.

The simplest version of this mistake:

    struct Node {
        me: Node   // ERROR: Node can't hold a Node by value
    }

The same problem shows up in a less obvious form when two or more structs
hold each other:

    struct A {
        b: B       // A holds a B by value
    }
    struct B {
        a: A       // ...and B holds an A by value -- the cycle closes here
    }

Neither struct is individually self-referential, but computing A's size
requires knowing B's size, which requires knowing A's size again. The
compiler reports the whole chain (`cycle: A -> B -> A`) so you can see
exactly which fields form the loop, not just the first struct it happened
to notice while checking.

An array of a struct counts the same way, since an array's size is just its
element size times its length:

    struct A {
        bs: B[2]   // still by value -- 2 copies of B live directly inside A
    }

The fix is almost always the same: change ONE of the fields in the cycle
from holding the struct directly to holding a pointer or reference to it
instead. A pointer is always the same size (one machine word) no matter
what it points to, so it breaks the "I need to know your size to know my
size" chain completely -- and this is also the normal, intended way to
write a self-referential data structure like a linked list or a tree:

    struct Node {
        value: int,
        next: Node*    // fixed-size pointer -- this is fine
    }

    struct A {
        b: &B          // a safe reference works just as well here
    }
    struct B {
        a: A
    }

Any one of `Node*` (raw pointer), `&Node` (non-null safe reference), or
`&?Node` (nullable safe reference) fixes this -- pick whichever fits how
the field is actually used elsewhere in your code. You only need to change
ONE field in the cycle; the others can stay exactly as they are.

codes.explanation:
A radix prefix isn't followed by any digit

Turf lets you write integers in hexadecimal (`0x`), binary (`0b`), and octal
(`0o`) as well as ordinary decimal:

    mut hex: int = 0xFF;    // 255
    mut bin: int = 0b1010;  // 10
    mut oct: int = 0o17;    // 15

Each of these prefixes has to be followed by at least one real digit in
that base. If it isn't -- because you stopped typing partway through, or
left a stray `0x`/`0b`/`0o` somewhere in your code -- there's nothing for
the compiler to actually build a number out of:

    mut x: int = 0x;   // ERROR: nothing after '0x'

The fix is almost always just finishing the literal you meant to write:

    mut x: int = 0xFF;

If you didn't mean to write a hex/binary/octal number at all, remove the
prefix and write a plain decimal number instead.
codes.name: MalformedRadixPrefixError
codes.title: Malformed radix prefix

codes.explanation:
A digit doesn't belong in this number's base

Once you write `0x`, `0b`, or `0o`, every digit that follows has to be a
valid digit in that particular base:

  - Hexadecimal (`0x`) allows 0-9 and a-f (or A-F).
  - Binary (`0b`) allows only 0 and 1.
  - Octal (`0o`) allows only 0-7.

This error means one of the characters right after the prefix isn't valid
for the base you chose -- most often a simple typo:

    mut x: int = 0b012;   // ERROR: `2` is not a valid digit in `0b`, which is binary (0-1)
    mut y: int = 0o8;     // ERROR: `8` is not a valid digit in `0o`, which is octal (0-7)
    mut z: int = 0xZZ;    // ERROR: `Z` is not a valid digit in `0x`, which is hexadecimal (0-9, a-f)

The fix depends on what you actually meant:

  - If you mistyped a digit, correct it:

        mut x: int = 0b010;   // fixed

  - If you actually wanted a plain decimal number, drop the prefix
    entirely:

        mut y: int = 8;   // no '0o' needed for an ordinary decimal number

Double-check which base you meant to use, and that every digit you typed
is one that base actually has.

codes.explanation:
An exponent marker with nothing after it

A `double` literal can use scientific-notation shorthand -- an `e` or `E`
followed by the power of ten to multiply by:

    mut avogadro: double = 6.022e23;
    mut tiny: double = 1.5e-3;      // 0.0015
    mut big: double = 1E+10;        // 10000000000.0

The letter `e`/`E` always has to be followed by an actual exponent: an
optional `+` or `-`, then at least one digit. Once Turf sees `e`/`E` right
after a number, it commits to reading an exponent -- it will never quietly
reinterpret it as something else, so leaving it unfinished is always an
error rather than the number just ending early:

    mut x: double = 1.5e;    // ERROR: `1.5e` has an exponent marker with no exponent after it.
    mut y: double = 1.5e+;   // ERROR: '+' with no digit after it
    mut z: double = 1e_5;    // ERROR: I cannot start a run of digits with `_` (E072).

The fix is to either finish the exponent:

    mut x: double = 1.5e3;   // 1500.0

...or, if you didn't mean to write an exponent at all, remove the `e`.

codes.explanation:
An integer literal can't be represented exactly as a 'double'

Turf allows an integer literal to implicitly become a 'double':

    mut d: double = 5;   // fine -- 5 converts to 5.0 exactly

But not every integer has an exact 'double' representation. A 'double'
only has 53 bits of precision, so a large-enough integer literal can't be
converted without silently losing its exact value:

    mut d: double = 9223372036854775807;
    // ERROR: this doesn't round-trip exactly as a double

Turf refuses this rather than silently rounding, because the whole point
of this check is to stop a number from silently becoming a slightly
different number.

The fix is one of:
  - Use 'int' instead, if you need the exact integer value.
  - Write it as an explicit float literal ('9223372036854775807.0') if
    you're fine with the (slightly rounded) double value.
codes.name: IntegerLiteralNotExactAsDoubleError
codes.title: Integer literal not exact as double

codes.explanation:
A float literal is too large -- it rounds to infinity

    mut d: double = 1e400;
    // ERROR: The literal `1e400` is too large for a `double`, which holds up to about 1.8e308.

'double' is an IEEE-754 double-precision float, which can represent
roughly up to ~1.8 * 10^308. A literal bigger than that has no finite
'double' value to become, so Turf rejects it outright instead of silently
handing you 'inf'.

This is about the LITERAL itself -- computing 'inf' at runtime (e.g. by
dividing/multiplying variables) is still allowed and behaves as ordinary
IEEE-754 floating point.

The fix is almost always a typo in the exponent, or the value genuinely
doesn't belong in a 'double'.

codes.explanation:
A generic instantiation chain never bottoms out

    fn<T> wrap(x: T) {
        wrap(Box { val: x });   // ERROR: every call asks for a NEW, bigger
    }                            // instantiation of wrap -- this never ends

Turf's generics are monomorphized: calling a generic function or
constructing a generic struct with a new combination of concrete types
compiles a brand new specialized copy of it. That's normally invisible --
`List<int>` and `List<string>` just work, each with its own compiled code.

But a generic that calls itself with a type that keeps growing (here,
`wrap<T>` always calls `wrap<Box<T>>`) would need an infinite number of
distinct compiled copies: wrap<int>, wrap<Box<int>>, wrap<Box<Box<int>>>,
forever. The compiler stops once a chain of instantiations requesting each
other is 64 deep rather than exhausting memory trying to finish, and prints
that chain (starting at the call in your own code) so you can see exactly
which call keeps growing the type. Independent calls never add up toward the
limit: calling one generic function on a hundred different types is a hundred
chains of length one. (A generic that keeps requesting more than one new
instantiation per level hits a separate, much larger cap on the total, and
says "too many generic instantiations" instead.)

This is almost never what you actually want. If you're trying to write a
recursive data structure or algorithm, use a pointer/reference
(`T*`/`&T`) so the TYPE stays fixed across the recursion -- only the VALUE
recurses, not the instantiation.
codes.name: GenericInstantiationDepthError
codes.title: Generic instantiation limit exceeded

codes.explanation:
You declared an operator between two types your module doesn't own

    // In module "geometry":
    struct Vec2 { x: int, y: int }
    operator +(a: Vec2, b: Vec2): Vec2 { ... }   // fine -- geometry owns Vec2

    // In some OTHER, unrelated module:
    operator +(a: SomeoneElsesType, b: AnotherModulesType): SomeoneElsesType {
        ...
    }
    // ERROR: this module owns neither SomeoneElsesType nor AnotherModulesType

An operator declaration needs at least one of its operands to be a struct
or enum declared in the SAME module (or main file) as the `operator`
itself. Without this rule, a third module could quietly redefine what `+`
(or any other operator) means between two types it has nothing to do with
-- and whether that redefinition took effect would depend on whether that
third module happened to be imported anywhere in the program, and in what
order. That's the kind of thing that works fine while you're writing the
code and then breaks mysteriously six months later when someone adds an
unrelated import.

To fix it, do one of:

  - Move the operator declaration into the module that actually declares
    one of the two types.
  - If you don't own either type and still need this behavior, write it as
    an ordinary named function instead (`fn add_vecs(a: Vec2, b: Vec2):
    Vec2`) -- there's no rule against that, only against redefining an
    OPERATOR on types you don't own.

This check doesn't apply to a builtin/`string` operand at all -- `string`
isn't "declared" by any one module the way a struct or enum is, so
`lib/std/core/strings.tr`'s own `operator +(a: string, b: string): string`
and friends are unaffected by this rule.

codes.explanation:
A module name matches more than one file

    // app/list.tr exists, and so does the standard library's list
    import list;
    // ERROR: I found 2 different files that answer to the module name `list`.
    //     standard library  <install>/lib/std/collections/list.tr
    //     next to main.tr   ./list.tr
    //   Hint: Rename ./list.tr (for example to `my_list.tr`) and import it by
    //   the new name. A module may not share its name with a
    //   standard-library module.

`import m;` names a module, not a file, and the compiler looks for `m.tr` in
four places: the standard library, installed packages (lib/usr), the
directory of the file that contains the import, and the current directory.
Exactly one of them must hold it.

Every place is checked, and none takes precedence over another: if two of
them have a `json.tr`, there is no rule that quietly picks one, because a
program could then run code its author did not write without anyone noticing.
A name that more than one file answers to is this error, listing each file.

In a project (`turf build`, `turf test`), the places are different: the
package's own modules anywhere under its src/, its direct dependencies, and
the standard library; a test also sees the `*_module.tr` helpers in tests/.
Two files called `report.tr` anywhere under src/ are this error too.

The fix depends on what collided:

- Your file and a standard-library module: rename your file. The standard
  library's name is not yours to change, and a program that imports the
  standard library's module must be able to say so.
- Two of your own files (for example one next to the importing file and one
  in the directory you ran the compiler from): rename one, or delete the one
  you did not mean.

The same file reached twice (when you compile from the file's own directory,
"next to the file" and "the current directory" are the same place) is one
match, not two.

An import written inside the standard library always means the standard
library's module. So a local list.tr never breaks a program that does not
import `list` itself, even though the standard library uses its own `list`
internally.

codes.explanation:
A `compare` header is not a legal pattern

    struct Point { x: int, y: int }

    compare p {
        matches Point { x }:          // ERROR: This pattern does not mention the field `y` of `Point`.
        matches Point { x: 1 + 2, .. }: // ERROR: a field pattern can't be an expression
        matches Q { x, .. }:          // ERROR: the value is a Point, not a Q
    }
    //   Hint: List every field, or end the pattern with `..` to ignore the
    //   ones you don't need: `Point { x, .. }`.

A `matches` header can be a plain value (`matches 3:`), `_`, a struct
pattern (`Point { x: 0, y }`), and any of those followed by a guard
(`... if x == y:`). One error code covers every way such a header can be
wrong; the message says which, and the hint says what to write instead:

- A struct pattern over a value that is not a struct, a struct of a different
  name, a field the struct does not have (that one is E068, with spelling
  suggestions), or a `&?T` / raw pointer subject.
- A field left out without `..`. Every field is listed, or the pattern ends in
  `..`, so adding a field to the struct later can't silently change what the
  pattern means.
- A field pattern that is not a literal (int, char, string, bool), an enum
  variant, `_`, a name to bind or a nested struct pattern. To compare a field
  with a variable or any other expression, bind it and use a guard:

      matches Point { x, .. } if x == limit:

  A `double` literal is never a pattern; test it in a guard too.
- A name bound twice in one pattern (`Point { x, y: x }`), or a field listed
  twice.
- Stacked `matches` headers that bind different names or different types.
  Stacked headers share one body, so the body reads one variable per name:

      matches Point { x: 0, y }:
      matches Point { x: 1, y }:     // ok: both bind y
          ...

- A guard that is not a `bool`.
- A lone `_` used as a variable, parameter or function name. `_` is the
  wildcard; `_name` (an underscore followed by anything) is an ordinary name,
  and is never reported as unused.

Inside a destructuring pattern a bare identifier always binds. At the top of a
header it is still a variable compared by equality, exactly as before patterns
existed.

An error value can be matched too: `IOError::Denied(path, mode)` destructures
a variant's payload positionally, inside a `compare` over an error (the `err`
of `recover as err run`, or a value of a declared error type). Its
sub-patterns are a struct pattern's -- a name that binds, `_`, a literal, an
enum variant, a nested struct pattern -- and, like a struct pattern, it lists
every field or ends in `..`:

    matches IOError::Denied(path, ..):     // ok
    matches IOError::Denied(path):         // ERROR: doesn't mention 'mode'
    matches IOError::NotFound:             // ERROR: it has a field; write (..)
    matches IOError::Timeout:              // ok: no fields, matched by tag

More ways such a header can be wrong: matching an error-variant pattern against
a value that is not an error, naming the variant of a different error type than
a declared-error subject holds, or empty parentheses (`IOError::NotFound()`).

codes.explanation:
An arm of a `compare` can never run

    compare p {
        matches _:               // matches everything
            ...
        done
        matches Point { x: 3 }:  // WARNING: This arm can never run.
            ...
        done
    }

Arms are tried in source order and the first header that matches wins. An
unguarded header that matches every value (`_`, or a struct pattern whose
fields are all bindings or `_`) therefore makes every later arm, and
`otherwise`, unreachable. This is a warning rather than an error: the dead arm
is harmless and often left behind while editing. Delete it, or move it above
the catch-all.

A guarded header doesn't count as a catch-all, because its guard may be false.
A duplicate value pattern (`matches 1:` twice) is a different and still
hard error: see E133.
codes.name: UnreachableArmWarning
codes.title: Unreachable compare arm

codes.explanation:
`try` used where it cannot work

    error IOError { NotFound(path: string) }
    fn open(p: string): !int { ... }

    fn main(): int {
        immut n: int = try open("x");   // ERROR: `main` returns an `int`, so `try` has nowhere to return an error to.
        return n;
    }
    //   Hint: Handle the error here instead: `f() recover as err run { ... }`.

`try e` passes the error of `e` on: if `e` (a `!T`) failed, `try` returns that
same error value -- same variant, same payload, same message -- from the
function it is written in, after running that function's pending `defer`s
exactly as a `return` would. On success it is just the value. So it needs:

- **A function that returns `!V`** (any `V`). `main` returns `int`, so nothing can
  fail out of it: handle the error there with `recover`. A function returning a
  plain type can be declared `!T` to let errors leave it.
- **A place a `return` is allowed.** A `defer` runs while the function is
  already returning, so a `try` anywhere inside one is an error. Handle the
  error inside the deferred statement: `defer f() recover run { ... };`.
- **A fallible operand.** `try plain()` where `plain` returns an `int` has no
  error to pass on; drop the `try`.
- **A function.** There is no function to return from at the top level.

`try` is a reserved word, and binds like a prefix operator: `try a() + try b()`
is `(try a()) + (try b())`.
codes.name: TryMisuseError
codes.title: Misplaced try

codes.explanation:
An error variant's payload is declared or used wrongly

    error IOError {
        NotFound(path: string),
        Denied(path: string, mode: int),
        Timeout
    }

    IOError::NotFound("a.txt")             // ok
    IOError::NotFound("a.txt", "message")  // ok: fields, then a string message
    IOError::Denied("a.txt")               // ERROR: declares 2 fields, given 1
    IOError::Denied("a.txt", "rw")         // ERROR: 'mode' is an int
    IOError::NotFound                      // ERROR: has fields, so it isn't a value
    //   Hint: Pass one argument per field, in order: 'IOError::Denied(...)'
    //   takes 2, or 3 with a trailing 'string' message.

A variant may declare typed fields, written `Name(field: Type, ...)`. A variant
with *N* fields is built with *N* arguments, or *N+1* when the extra trailing
argument is the `string` message (`err.message` still reads it). A variant with
no fields is written without parentheses and takes no arguments, or exactly
one, its message -- as it always did.

A payload is read only by destructuring it in a `compare`:

    compare err {
        matches IOError::NotFound(path):   ...
        matches IOError::Denied(path, _):  ...
        otherwise:                         ...
    }

What this code reports:

- Empty parentheses in a declaration (`NotFound()`), a field with no type
  (`NotFound(path)`), or a field name used twice in one variant.
- A field whose type is an error type, a `!T` or `void`: an error value carries
  data about what went wrong, not another failure.
- A constructor call with the wrong number of arguments, or an argument whose
  type is not its field's (or, past the fields, not a `string` message).
- A bare `IOError::NotFound` where a value is wanted, for a variant that has
  fields: without its payload there is no value. It is still fine as an `==`
  or `!=` operand (`err == IOError::NotFound`, which compares the variant only)
  and as the head of a pattern.

An unknown field type is the ordinary unknown-type error, and a pattern that
does not fit its variant is E092.
codes.name: ErrorPayloadError
codes.title: Invalid error payload
