codes.explanation:
A string or character was opened but never closed

Text in Turf is wrapped in quotes: `"hello"` for a string, `'a'` for a single character. This error means Turf found the opening quote and then ran out of line (or out of file) before it found the matching closing one.

    mut greeting: string = "hello;       // the closing " is missing
    mut letter: char = 'a;                // the closing ' is missing

Add the missing quote:

    mut greeting: string = "hello";
    mut letter: char = 'a';

Two things worth knowing:

- A string can't continue onto the next line. If you want a line break inside your text, write `\n` in it: `"first line\nsecond line"`.
- A quote inside your text needs a backslash in front of it, or Turf thinks the text has ended there: `"she said \"hi\""`.

When this error appears, look at the line it points to first. Very often the quote is right there, one character short of where you meant it to be.
codes.name: UnterminatedLiteralError
codes.title: Unterminated string or character literal

codes.explanation:
Turf doesn't know that escape sequence

Inside a string or a character, a backslash `\` starts an "escape sequence": a short code for something you can't easily type, like a line break. Turf knows exactly these:

    \n   a new line          \t   a tab
    \r   carriage return     \0   the null character
    \\   a backslash         \"   a double quote
    \'   a single quote      \a \b \f \v   the rarer control characters

Anything else after a backslash is an error, because Turf would otherwise have to guess what you meant:

    mut path: string = "C:\temp\q";     // \q is not an escape sequence

If you wanted a real backslash character, write it twice:

    mut path: string = "C:\\temp\\q";

Most often this error is a Windows-style path or a regular expression with single backslashes in it. Double each backslash and it goes away.
codes.name: InvalidEscapeSequenceError
codes.title: Invalid escape sequence

codes.explanation:
A character literal must hold exactly one character

A `char` is a single character, written between single quotes: `'a'`. Turf found something between the quotes that isn't exactly one character -- either nothing at all, or more than one.

    mut empty: char = '';       // nothing between the quotes
    mut two: char = 'ab';       // two characters

A character literal holds exactly one:

    mut letter: char = 'a';

If you wanted several characters, you want a string, which uses double quotes:

    mut word: string = "ab";

An escape sequence like `'\n'` is still one character (a new line), so that is fine. And if you meant a single quote itself, write `'\''`.
codes.name: InvalidCharLiteralError
codes.title: Invalid character literal

codes.name: MissingSemicolonError
codes.title: Missing semicolon

codes.explanation:
Turf found something it didn't expect here

This is the "that doesn't belong there" error: Turf was in the middle of reading something and ran into a token that can't legally appear at this spot. It names the token, so start by looking at it.

The usual causes:

- A value or operand that was left out:

      mut x: int = ;
      mut y: int = 5 + ;

- An extra `;` right after something that has already ended, such as a loop:

      do { x = x - 1; } while (x > 0);;       // the second ; has nothing to end

- A keyword where a value was expected -- `if`, `while` and friends are statements, not values:

      mut x: int = while;

- A stray character that isn't part of Turf, or an `@` that isn't `@caller_location` (the only decorator Turf has).

- A declaration keyword in the wrong place. A top-level `mut x: int = 5;` outside any function is not a declaration Turf accepts: variables live inside functions (a constant you want to share across files is `pub immut`).

Delete the stray token, or add what was supposed to be there, and the error goes away. If the highlighted spot looks fine, check the line just above it: an unclosed bracket earlier on is often what makes a later, perfectly good token look wrong.
codes.name: UnexpectedTokenError
codes.title: Unexpected token

codes.name: UnclosedDelimiterError
codes.title: Unclosed bracket, brace or parenthesis

codes.explanation:
A comma is missing

Turf was reading a list -- the fields of a struct, the variants of an enum, the arguments of a call, the items of an array -- and found a second item without a comma in front of it. (The message says what it was looking for: usually "`,` or the closing bracket".)

    struct Point {
        x: int
        y: int           // no comma after `x: int`
    }

    add(1 2)             // no comma between the arguments

Separate the items with commas:

    struct Point {
        x: int,
        y: int
    }

    add(1, 2)

It can also mean the list was supposed to end and the closing bracket is missing (see E104); the message names both possibilities because from where Turf stands it can't tell which one you meant. A trailing comma after the last item is fine.
codes.name: MissingCommaError
codes.title: Missing comma

codes.name: MissingColonError
codes.title: Missing colon

codes.name: MissingOpeningDelimiterError
codes.title: Missing opening brace or parenthesis

codes.explanation:
A name was expected here

Turf was waiting for a name -- of a variable, function, parameter, struct, field, enum variant, module -- and found something that isn't one. The message says which name it was looking for and after what.

    mut : int = 5;               // a variable needs a name
    fn (a: int): int { ... }     // a function needs a name
    struct { x: int }            // so does a struct
    import ;                     // so does an import

Give it one:

    mut count: int = 5;
    fn add(a: int): int { ... }

A name must start with a letter or an underscore, and it can't be one of Turf's reserved words (`if`, `fn`, `run`, `step`, `ptr`, ...). If you used a reserved word as a name, Turf reads it as the keyword and complains that the name is missing: rename it.
codes.name: ExpectedNameError
codes.title: Expected a name

codes.explanation:
A type was expected here

Turf was waiting for a type -- `int`, `string`, `bool`, `double`, `char`, a struct's name, `List<int>`, ... -- and found something that isn't one.

    fn add(a: int, b:): int { ... }        // parameter `b` has no type
    fn get(): { ... }                       // the return type is missing
    mut values: List<> = ...;               // nothing between the < >

Write the type:

    fn add(a: int, b: int): int { ... }

A function that returns nothing says so with `void`: `fn log(msg: string): void { ... }`. A type name is case sensitive -- `Int` is not `int` -- and a struct or enum you declared works as a type too.

`sizeof` takes a type too, not a value: `sizeof(a)` with a variable `a` is this error. Write the variable's type, `sizeof(int)`.
codes.name: ExpectedTypeError
codes.title: Expected a type

codes.explanation:
A specific word or symbol was expected

Turf was in the middle of a construct that has a fixed shape and found something other than the next fixed piece. The message names the exact word or symbol it wanted.

A few of the fixed shapes:

    for i in 0..10 { ... }               // `in` after the loop variable
    do { ... } while keep_going;          // `while` after a do-block
    give a otherwise b                   // `otherwise` after `give`
    compare x { matches 1: ... }         // `matches` or `otherwise` in a compare
    value recover run { ... };           // `run`, `produce` or `as` after `recover`
    extern fn malloc(n: int): ptr;       // `fn` after `extern`
    pub immut MAX: int = 3;           // `immut` after `export`
    machine Door { Open -> Closed }      // `->` between two states

Compare what you wrote with the shape above and add or fix the piece the message asks for. If you wrote a lookalike (a `then` instead of `{`, `:=` instead of `=`), that is the one to change: Turf has no alias for it.

One shape is a generic function's type arguments written without `::`. `identity<int>(3)` reads as `identity < int ...`, and `int` cannot be compared, so this is E110. Type arguments of a generic function follow `::`, and the compiler prints the fix:

    immut a: int = identity<int>(3);      // E110
    immut a: int = identity::<int>(3);    // fine
codes.name: ExpectedKeywordError
codes.title: Expected a specific word or symbol

codes.name: NestingTooDeepError
codes.title: Nested too deeply

codes.explanation:
`void` can't be the type of a variable, field or parameter

`void` means "nothing". It describes a function that gives nothing back, so it can only appear as a function's return type:

    fn log(msg: string): void { ... }        // fine

A variable, a struct field or a parameter holds a value, and "nothing" can't be held:

    mut x: void;                  // what would x contain?
    struct Box { item: void }
    fn show(thing: void): void { ... }

Give it a real type -- `int`, `string`, a struct, ... If you need a pointer to something whose type you don't know (in `extern` code), use `ptr` or `void*` instead.
codes.name: VoidTypeNotAllowedError
codes.title: void used as a type

codes.explanation:
That syntax used to exist, but doesn't any more

Turf changed. The form you wrote was valid in an earlier version, and now it is an error with a pointer to what replaced it. The message says which.

Struct creation moved from a brace literal to a call:

    mut p: Point = Point { x: 1, y: 2 };      // removed
    mut p: Point = Point::new(1, 2);          // a struct with a constructor
    mut p: Point = Point::default();          // every field zeroed

Static methods moved from `::` in the declaration to a `static` marker on the method:

    fn Point::origin(): Point { ... }         // removed
    static fn Point.origin(): Point { ... }

If you are following an old tutorial or an example you found online, this is the usual cause: the example predates the change.
codes.name: RemovedSyntaxError
codes.title: Syntax that no longer exists

codes.name: DuplicateMemberError
codes.title: Duplicate member

codes.name: InvalidOperatorDeclarationError
codes.title: Invalid operator declaration

codes.name: ExternFunctionBodyError
codes.title: extern function with a body

codes.name: InvalidErrorDeclarationError
codes.title: Invalid error declaration

codes.name: StatementOutsideFunctionError
codes.title: Statement outside a function

codes.explanation:
There is no `main` function

A program has to say where it starts. In Turf that is a function called `main` that returns an `int`:

    fn main(): int {
        return 0;
    }

Turf found no such function in the file you compiled, so it has nothing to run.

Usual causes:

- The function is missing, or misspelled (`Main`, `mian`). The name is case sensitive.
- It isn't the file you meant to compile. A project's entry point is `src/main.tr`.
- The file is a module -- a library of functions that other files `import` -- and was never meant to run on its own. A module doesn't need a `main`. To check one without running it: `turf check --module file.tr`.

The number `main` returns is the program's exit status; `0` means success.
codes.name: MissingEntryPointError
codes.title: No main function

codes.explanation:
That loop form isn't supported

Turf has two kinds of `for` loop, and they take different shapes:

    for i in 0..10 step i += 1 { ... }          // a counting loop: ONE variable and a range
    for value in numbers { ... }                // for-each over an array
    for (index, value) in numbers { ... }       // for-each that also gives you the position

The `(index, value)` pair only makes sense when you walk an array, because a range like `0..10` *is* the index -- there is no second thing to bind:

    for (i, x) in 0..10 { ... }                 // not supported

Pick the form that matches what you are looping over: a range gets a single variable; an array can get one or two.
codes.name: InvalidLoopFormError
codes.title: Unsupported loop form

codes.explanation:
The compiler hit a problem of its own

This one isn't about your code. Turf reached a state that its earlier checks should have made impossible -- a type that was never resolved, a field lookup on something that isn't a struct -- and stopped, rather than guess and risk producing a program that does the wrong thing.

It is a bug in the compiler, not a mistake you made, and it is worth reporting.

What helps most when you report it:

- the smallest piece of code that still prints this message (cut lines until it stops, then put the last one back),
- the full text of the error, including the line and column,
- the output of `turf --version`.

In the meantime a small change to the code around the line it points to -- naming an intermediate value with `mut`, adding a type annotation -- often steps around it.
codes.name: InternalCompilerError
codes.title: Internal compiler error

codes.explanation:
Turf can't take the address of that

`&x` gives you a reference to something that lives in memory, so it only works on things that have a place: a variable, a struct field, or an array element.

    mut x: int = 5;
    mut r: &int = &x;                 // a variable: fine
    mut p: &int = &point.x;           // a field: fine
    mut q: &int = &numbers[2];        // an array element: fine

A computed result has no place -- it is a temporary value that disappears -- so there is nothing to point at:

    mut r: &int = &(x + 1);           // (x + 1) is a value, not a place
    mut r: &int = &compute();         // so is a function's result

Store the value in a variable first, then take the address of the variable:

    mut tmp: int = x + 1;
    mut r: &int = &tmp;
codes.name: NonAddressableExpressionError
codes.title: Cannot take the address of this

codes.explanation:
An array's size has to be a positive whole number

An array is declared with a fixed size written in square brackets, and that size is a count of slots, so it must be a whole number greater than zero:

    mut numbers: int[5];             // five slots

These are rejected:

    mut empty: int[0];               // an array with no slots can hold nothing
    mut negative: int[-3];           // you can't have -3 slots
    mut half: int[2.5];              // slots come in whole numbers

The size can also come from a literal: `mut nums: int[] = [1, 2, 3];` is exactly `int[3]`. An empty literal has no size to give, so it is the same mistake:

    mut a: int[] = [];               // 'a' has no size -- an array needs at least one element

Give it at least one element, or write the size yourself (`mut a: int[5];`).

If you don't know how many items you will need in advance, an array is the wrong tool: `List<T>` (from `import list;`) grows as you add to it.
codes.name: InvalidArraySizeError
codes.title: Invalid array size

codes.explanation:
Those two values can't be compared

`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` ask a question about two values, and Turf can only answer it when the two are the same kind of thing and that kind knows how to be compared. This error means one of those conditions failed. The message names the two types.

Comparing different kinds of value:

    mut x: int = 5;
    if x == null { ... }          // an int is never null, so this can never be true
    if x == "5" { ... }           // a number and a string

Compare like with like -- `x == 5`, `name == "Ada"`. Only pointers and references can be compared to `null`; a plain `int`, `double`, `bool` or `string` can never be null.

Comparing structs directly isn't supported yet:

    if a == b { ... }             // a and b are both Point

Compare the fields you care about instead:

    if a.x == b.x && a.y == b.y { ... }

Putting enum values in order isn't supported either, because the order of variants isn't something a program should rely on. Convert to numbers first if you really mean it:

    if (a to int) < (b to int) { ... }
codes.name: InvalidComparisonError
codes.title: Values can't be compared

codes.explanation:
More than one definition fits this call equally well

Turf found the function or operator you used -- twice. Two definitions both match this call *exactly*, so Turf can't know which one you mean, and it refuses to guess: the answer would depend on the order of your imports, which is the kind of thing that silently changes when someone reorders two lines.

The usual way to meet it is two modules that each define the same helper:

    import ufcs_ambiguous_a_module;     // defines describe_int(n: int)
    import ufcs_ambiguous_b_module;     // defines describe_int(n: int) too

    mut r: string = n.describe_int();   // which one?

Any of these removes the ambiguity:

- Remove one of the two imports, if you don't need both.
- Import only the names you want from each: `import a::[describe_int];`.
- Call the one you mean through its module: `a::describe_int(n)`.
- Rename one of the definitions, if you wrote both.

Operators have the same rule: if two visible `operator+(Vec, Vec)` definitions exist, `a + b` is ambiguous until one of them goes.

An overloaded name used as a function value (`mut f: fn(int, int): int = combine;` with two `combine`s) is this error too: there is no single signature to take, and the variable's type does not pick one. Write a function with its own name that calls the overload you want, and use that.
codes.name: AmbiguousCallError
codes.title: Ambiguous call

codes.name: UnsupportedOperationError
codes.title: Operation not supported here

codes.explanation:
That number isn't one of the enum's values

An enum is a fixed list of named values. Converting a number to an enum only makes sense for the numbers that correspond to a variant: the first variant is `0`, the next `1`, and so on.

    enum Color { Red, Green }         // Red is 0, Green is 1

    mut c: Color = 1 to Color;        // fine -- Green
    mut d: Color = 7 to Color;        // there is no variant number 7

Turf checks a literal number at compile time and tells you the valid range (here 0 to 1), so a mistake like this never reaches your running program.

Usually the better fix is to skip the number entirely and use the variant by name:

    mut c: Color = Color::Green;

If you are converting a number you computed or read in, check that it is in range first -- a value that isn't a variant has no sensible meaning.
codes.name: EnumValueOutOfRangeError
codes.title: Enum value out of range

codes.explanation:
This variable needs a starting value

Some declarations can't exist without a value. Turf found one that has none.

An `immutable` variable can never be assigned after it is created, so it has to get its one and only value right where it is declared:

    immutable PI: double;             // never gets a value, and can't later

    immutable PI: double = 3.14159;

`guess` asks Turf to work out the type from the value, so it has nothing to work with if there isn't one:

    mut x: guess;                     // guess from what?

    mut x: guess = 5;                 // an int

An array of non-null references, such as `(&Node)[3]`, or an unsized local array `int[]`, also needs a value, since there is no zero element to start from. A fixed-size array of numbers, strings or `&?T` needs none: its elements start as zero.

Either give the variable its value, or -- for a `mut` variable whose value comes later -- say its type instead of using `guess`:

    mut x: int;
    x = 5;

`guess` only works on a local variable that is given its value on the same line. A function's parameters, its return type and a struct's fields have no value to look at, so there you always write the type:

    fn double_it(x: guess): int { ... }       // x: guess has nothing to infer from
    fn double_it(x: int): int { ... }

    struct Counter { count: guess }           // so does a field
    struct Counter { count: int }
codes.name: MissingInitializerError
codes.title: Missing initializer

codes.explanation:
There is nothing to work the type out from

`guess` means "use whatever type the value on the right has". That only works when the value has a real type to offer. Turf found one that doesn't:

    mut a: guess = null;              // `null` could be a reference to anything
    mut b: guess = print_it();        // print_it() returns void: no value, no type
    mut c: guess = List::default();   // which kind of List?

Say the type yourself, the same way you would without `guess`, or, for a generic struct, where the value is built:

    mut a: &?Point = null;
    mut c: List<int> = List::default();
    mut d = List<int>::default();     // the same List<int>

When a constructor's arguments decide the type arguments (`mut b = Box::new(42);`, a `Box<int>`), the compiler prints that one as a fix: `Box<int>::new(42)`.

For the `void` case, the real problem is usually that the function was supposed to return something. Call it as a statement on its own if you only want what it does:

    print_it();

The same error is reported at a generic function whose type parameter no parameter mentions. Every type parameter has to appear in a parameter, so a call can always work it out from its arguments; `T` here appears in none:

    fn<T> make(): T { ... }           // which T would `make()` be?

Use the type parameter in a parameter (`fn<T> make(seed: T): T`), or drop it and name a real type.
codes.name: NothingToInferError
codes.title: Nothing to infer a type from

codes.name: RawPointerOutsideUnsafeError
codes.title: Raw pointer outside unsafe

codes.explanation:
That type has no methods

A "method call" is `thing.method(...)`. A struct can declare methods, so `p.length()` works on a `Point` that defines `length`. An `int`, a `bool` or a `double` has no methods of its own, so there is nothing for the dot to find:

    mut x: int = 5;
    x.foo();                          // an int has no `foo`

Usually one of three things is going on:

- The name is misspelled, or it is a function in a module you meant to import. Many things are written `module::function(x)`, not `x.function()`: `math::abs(x)`.
- You called a method on the wrong variable.
- You meant a struct, and the variable's type isn't the struct you think it is.

An array has exactly two built-in methods, `length()` and `copy()`, and neither takes an argument. Anything else is this error too:

    mut a: int[3] = [1, 2, 3];
    a.copy(1);                        // 'copy()' on an array takes no arguments, but was given 1.
    a.reverse();                      // Arrays have no method 'reverse'.
    mut s: string = "abc";
    s.copy();                         // Cannot call method 'copy' on type 'string' -- only struct instances have methods.

(`copy()` is for arrays only. To take part of an array, slice it first: `a[1..3].copy()`.)

(`x.f()` does work on a non-struct when a function `f` taking that type is imported -- that is how `text.length()` works on a `string`. So check the spelling, and that the module is imported.)

A method declared on one of its own type parameters is this error too, at the declaration. In `fn<Holder> Holder.count()` the name `Holder` is the type parameter, not the struct, so it has no methods. Write `fn<T> Holder.count()` for `struct Holder<T>`.
codes.name: MethodOnNonStructError
codes.title: Method called on a non-struct

codes.name: InvalidRecoverError
codes.title: Invalid recover

codes.explanation:
The same value is matched twice in one `compare`

A `compare` tries its `matches` arms from top to bottom and runs the first one that fits. If a later arm matches a value an earlier arm already handles, the later arm can never run -- and Turf treats that as a mistake rather than letting dead code sit quietly, because it nearly always means one of the two arms was meant to match something else.

    compare day {
        matches 1: ... done
        matches 2: ... done
        matches 1: ... done          // 1 is already handled above
    }

Either change the repeated value to the one you meant, delete the extra arm, or -- if both arms should do the same thing -- stack them so they share one body:

    compare day {
        matches 1:
        matches 7: ... done          // 1 or 7
        matches 2: ... done
    }

(A different situation: an arm that can never run because an earlier *catch-all* arm matches everything -- `matches _:` -- is only a warning, E094.)
codes.name: DuplicateMatchArmError
codes.title: Duplicate matches pattern

codes.explanation:
That conversion isn't allowed

`value to Type` converts a value from one type to another, but only for conversions that have a clear meaning. Turf found one that doesn't, and names both types.

These are fine:

    mut d: double = 5 to double;        // a whole number to a decimal
    mut n: int = 3.9 to int;            // a decimal to a whole number (drops the .9)
    mut s: string = 42 to string;       // a number to text
    mut c: char = 65 to char;           // a character code to a character
    mut code: int = 'a' to int;         // and back
    mut p: Point = r to Point;          // copies the Point a `&Point` refers to

These are not:

    mut b: bool = 5 to bool;            // there is no "5 as true/false"
    mut n: int = true to int;           // a bool is not secretly 0 or 1

Say what you mean instead. If you want to know whether a number is zero, compare it: `n != 0`. If you want a number from a condition, choose the numbers: `give 1 otherwise 0`.
codes.name: InvalidCastError
codes.title: That conversion isn't allowed

codes.explanation:
That isn't something you can call

Writing `(...)` after a name means "run this". Turf found a name that is a plain value, not a function.

An enum variant is already a complete value. It doesn't take arguments:

    enum Color { Red, Green }

    mut c: Color = Color::Red();        // Red is a value, not a function
    mut c: Color = Color::Red;          // just the name

The same goes for an `error` variant that carries no payload fields: write `IOError::NotFound`, not `IOError::NotFound()` -- unless it takes a message, in which case you pass exactly one string: `IOError::NotFound("a.txt")`.

If you meant to build a struct, that is a call to its constructor: `Point::new(1, 2)` or `Point::default()`.
codes.name: NotCallableError
codes.title: Not callable

codes.name: InvalidModuleQualifierError
codes.title: Invalid module qualifier

codes.name: NotAValueError
codes.title: Not a value

codes.name: MissingTypeArgumentsError
codes.title: Missing type arguments

codes.explanation:
That isn't a valid number

A decimal number has exactly one `.`, with at least one digit after it:

    mut pi: double = 3.14;
    mut half: double = .5;           // the digit before the point is optional
    mut big: double = 6.022e23;      // the point comes before any exponent

Turf found a `.` in a place a number can't have one. The message says which of three it is.

**A second decimal point.** `3.14.15` looks like two numbers run together -- `3.14` and `.15` -- and Turf won't guess which one you meant:

    mut x: double = 3.14.15;         // ERROR: a number can have only one '.'
    mut y: double = 1e5.5;           // ERROR: the point goes BEFORE the exponent

If you meant one decimal, remove a point. If you meant two values, put a comma or an operator between them: `3.14 + 0.15`.

**A point with nothing after it.** `5.` is not a number, because a decimal needs a digit after the point:

    mut x: double = 5.;              // ERROR: '5.' ends in a '.'

Write `5.0` for the decimal or `5` for the whole number.

**A point on a hexadecimal, binary or octal number.** Those are whole numbers, so they have no fractional part:

    mut x: double = 0xFF.5;          // ERROR: hexadecimal numbers are whole numbers

Write the value as an ordinary decimal instead (`255.5`).

What is *not* an error: `1..5` is a range, not `1.` and `.5`, and a letter right after the point is a method call on the value (`5.abs()` is `abs` called on `5`), so neither is touched by this check.
codes.name: MalformedNumberError
codes.title: Malformed number

codes.name: UnsizedArrayPlacementError
codes.title: Unsized array where a size is needed

codes.name: ImmutableArrayWrittenThroughSliceError
codes.title: Immutable array passed to a function that changes it

codes.name: SliceOfNonArrayError
codes.title: Slicing something that isn't an array

codes.explanation:
A range slice's bounds are out of range

A slice `arr[start..end]` is a view of the elements from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. For the slice to make sense, both bounds must lie inside the array and `start` can't come after `end`: `0 <= start <= end <= length`. A negative bound counts back from the end, so `arr[-2..]` is the last two elements; the length is added to it before the check.

    immut a: int[3] = [1, 2, 3];
    immut t = a[1..4];                 // E143 -- the end (4) is past the length (3)
    immut u = a[-4..];                 // E143 -- -4 counts back past the first element
    immut w = a[2..1];                 // E143 -- start comes after end

`[2..1]` is not "empty", it's a mistake. An empty slice is `[i..i]`, and `a[3..]` on a 3-element array is also a valid empty slice, because `start == length` is allowed.

Turf reports this when it can prove it: constant bounds on an array of known size, or, for an `int[]` parameter whose length isn't known yet, a start that is after the end when both are constants of the same sign (`arr[3..1]`). When a bound is only known as the program runs, the check happens then instead, and a bad range stops the program with `Slice range out of bounds for 'arr'`.

To fix it, correct the bounds. If you want everything from a point on, leave the end out: `arr[2..]`.

codes.explanation:
A machine state has no way to be entered

A `machine` lists the transitions it allows. Turf counts the arrows that point INTO each state, and warns about any state that nothing points at:

    machine Door {
        Closed -> Open,
        Open -> Closed,
        Locked -> Closed,   // WARNING: Machine `Door` declares state `Locked` with no incoming transitions.
    }

Once a `Door` leaves its starting value, there is no arrow that can bring it to `Locked`, so every use of that state after the first move is dead weight. It is usually a forgotten edge. Add the arrow:

    machine Door {
        Closed -> Open,
        Open -> Closed,
        Locked -> Closed,
        Closed -> Locked,
    }

One case is a false positive: the state a machine STARTS in. A machine begins in whatever state you construct it with, so that state may legitimately have no incoming arrow, and Turf has no way to know which state you mean to start in. If `Locked` is only ever a starting state, the warning is expected and safe to ignore. Allowing the warning is the right tool for that.

This is a warning, not an error -- compilation still succeeds. To silence it for a whole build, set its lint level to allow: `turf build --allow E153` (or `[lints] E153 = "allow"` in turf.toml).

codes.explanation:
`export immut` is the old spelling of `pub immut`

A module constant is declared at the top level of a module with `immut`. Written `pub immut` (or `public immut`), other modules can use it as `module::NAME`; without `pub` it is private to its module:

    pub immut MAX_USERS: int = 100;   // module::MAX_USERS from an importer
    immut RETRIES: int = 3;           // only this module

`export immut` is the older spelling of `pub immut` and means the same:

    export immut MAX_USERS: int = 100;   // WARNING (E176 at `warn`)

The compiler's `Fix:` replaces `export` with `pub`.

This warning starts at `allow` in 2.3: turn it on with `turf build --warn E176` (or `[lints] E176 = "warn"` in turf.toml). TurfLang 3.0 removes `export`, and `turf migrate 3.0` rewrites it for you.
